utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I apologise for the delay. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I didn't hear anything. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will -- I will repeat the question. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, Senior Trial Attorney for the Prosecution team, together with Ms. Patricia Sellers and Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and the rest of the team. Appearances for the accused Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. Together with us are Ms. Jasmina Cosic, legal assistant, and Mr. Geoff Roberts, our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you, Ms. Vidovic, and the rest of your team. Are there any preliminary matters that you would like to raise before we bring in the first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There is a matter I need to raise with you in private session, but that can be done perhaps when the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Depends on what it is. On the part of the Defence, are there any preliminary matters that you would like to raise? Okay. Thank you. So we can bring the witness in. And I do apologise to everyone for having started with about 15 minutes delay late. The reason was technical. We couldn't -- we couldn't start before of technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when I say welcome to this Tribunal, I know that you work here, but welcome to this courtroom and to this trial. You are about to start giving evidence, and before you do so, as you know, because this is not the first time you have given evidence, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will, in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained on a piece of paper which Madam Usher is going to hand to you. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take -- take a chair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Di Fazio, I take it you will be conducting the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And can we just now very briefly go into private session? It's just a preliminary matter. It won't take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while. We should be in private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. So the witness is in your hands, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours please, can I now distribute her declaration and annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead. So I take it that this annex that I already had --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it is just an informal one which is not going to be part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. That hopefully represents today's end product.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. That's okay. The important thing is that we make it clear because I don't want in my files any documents that are not in reality tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can Your Honours let me know when you wish me to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Ms. Manas, I just want to go through some personal details of yours very briefly. I think you served in the South African police from 1983 to April of 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the South African police you reached the rank of super --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll slow down. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think you reached the rank of superintendent?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In April of 1995 did you come here to The Hague and take up employment in the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would you mind speaking up just a little. And you've essentially been here since April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You held the rank of investigator here at the Office of the Prosecutor from April 1995 until recently, August this year, when you were made acting team leader of team 9; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the course of your experience here at the Office of the Prosecutor, have you had experience in conducting missions where evidence is seized, documents, artefacts, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And has that been the case since April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And in the course of those missions, have you yourself seized documents?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I take it other forms of evidence, artefacts and so on?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And have you seen other investigators do the same?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In addition to investigators conducting seizures, do other employees of the OTP occasionally conduct seizures such as military experts?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, as well as lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So lawyers, investigators, military analysts sometimes seize documentation and other evidence in the field?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You're familiar, then, are you, with the procedures that are adopted when documentation and other forms of evidence is seized?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: [Inaudible].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And have you been present when documentation has been seized pursuant to search warrant or voluntarily handed over?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, one such mission. It was the Tuzla operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you aware -- you may not have personally experienced it, but are you aware of seizures where documentation is voluntarily handed over?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, in the field and on missions, seizure can be -- of a document can be of the original and can it be of a copy of the original?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true. In most of these cases they're mainly copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened -- that's the Chamber, I'm sorry, what happens when an officer of the OTP decides to seize or take custody of or receive a document in the field and he wants to take a copy of that document? What's the general procedure, please?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Are we talking about a single document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, we can start from the small and perhaps move on to the larger seizures. So let's start with the situation where it's a small number of documents or an individual document.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: During investigation or during an interview when a witness provide evidence which is related, the evidence -- the document is obtained from the witness. The investigator examines the document. In most cases it's the copy which is provided, and this -- this document is embodied in the witness statement fully describing what is in the document with the -- and as such it's annexed to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, perhaps you could ask the same -- put the same question in a different manner to the witness, because I don't think that this is precisely what we would like to -- to hear from the witness. The procedure that we are mostly interested in -- this is, of course, important, but the procedure that we are mostly interested in is what happens if an investigator goes to a particular village or town and enters a particular building where documents are seized. For example, if the investigator goes into a police station in a particular village where documents are being kept, irrespective of the relativity to a particular witness, what is the procedure that is followed? Because at that point in time, I would think it that the originals are seized and not copies. So that -- .

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That may not necessarily be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it may not necessarily be so. But perhaps she could go through all the procedure as it may vary from one case to another, but she's just restricted -- limited herself to the case when a witness is being interviewed and this witness hands over copies of originals. .

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's only part of the scenario -- .

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- which is much, much bigger. So now you've heard what I've said perhaps it's not matter of Mr. Di Fazio putting the question. You can enlighten us on these issues. I understand from other cases that you do have a standard policy and standard instructions on how to go about acquiring -- acquiring evidence, documents in particular. So please deal with the matter from beginning to end, different scenarios that you have on the ground when an investigator is involved in the acquisition of evidence. .

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours -- if Your Honour pleases, I understand your concern and with respect it's quite a good -- a very legitimate concern, and I intend to adduce evidence of precisely what is concerning you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I leave the witness in your hands. .

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This witness was in fact involved in just such a seizure and I intend to come to that to recount her personal experience and then ask her to comment if that's general practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. .

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So that was the way I was going to construct, so it I'll cover it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And conduct your examination-in-chief in the way which suits you best. .

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So we'll get to the larger seizures very shortly, but I'm now talking about small individual seizures, for example, from a witness who might be providing a statement. If that witness who is giving a statement to an investigator also provides documents, what is the procedure at that point of time when the documents are handed over to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, this is embodied in the statement describing the document given. It forms part of a receipt and is annexed to the statement. If the material or documents which is not relevant to the investigation or usually the investigator gives a receipt to the witness describing -- a receipt can be written by the investigators describing the contents that was handed over and a receipt is provided to the witness. And when a copy is handed over to -- the investigating officer examines the copy that was provided and to make sure that it's the true copy of the original, and he or she signs the reverse side of the document stating the same, whether it's a true version of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I want to move to a -- the larger operations that His Honour touched upon. But before I do that, can I just ask you to look at items 103 to 107 on your annex list. Now, I'm referring to the column that appears on the extreme left-hand side that at the top is headed with the words "pre-trial exhibit number." Do you see that column?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I'll ask you to comment on the actual structure of the spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 103 to 107, page 7 of the document. 103 to 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You see there that you have commented in the right-hand side that Steve Tedder seized the document from the Tuzla 2nd Corps collection. Tuzla collection, 7th of October, 2002. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you aware of that particular search and seizure and mission -- search and seizure operation, I should say, and mission?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you personally participate?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I participated in this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And were there a number of officers from the OTP involved in the particular mission?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of investigators, analysts, and lawyers involved in this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And it stretched over a number of days, I believe.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: The search took place one day, the actual search itself, and the examining of the documents was done the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And were many documents seized on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So I'd like you to address His Honour's question. Explain the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...because in the annex here the first of these documents indeed refer to the date 7 October 2002. Then 106 refers to 7 October 2003, and 107 refers to 7 October 2004. That is obviously a mistake, I would imagine, I mean, because I would imagine that they went back and on exactly the same day the following year and then again on the exactly the same day the following year to three subsequent years --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm grateful for Your Honour's eagle eye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that is, I presume, Ms. Manas, that that is to be corrected. No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's definitely an error --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in the dates. But it's 2002. It was the Tuzla mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks for correcting that. Now, can you tell Their Honours the procedure that was adopted on that occasion where large numbers of documents were being seized by officers in the field?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: This mission was a result of a search warrant which was issued by Judge Hunt in July of that year, and eventually it happened to be a consensual search. The whole team went to this 2nd Corps -- the 2nd Corps headquarters in Tuzla and the barracks in Tuzla. I can say it's -- Your Honours, just allow me to get the names of the places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just a moment. What are you referring to as you flick over?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: These are my notes relating to the document searches. If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Notes that you created in anticipation of testifying?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's right. Am I allowed to use these notes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Only with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The practice here is to allow this on -- on the condition that if any of the parties, either Defence or Prosecution, want to see those notes you need to make them available. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have no objection to the witness referring to her notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I suppose there is no objection on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly no objection. If the Defence wants a copy -- I don't have a copy with me, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's apparently not necessary. If it is necessary and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We would appreciate that, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps during the break if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, please refer to your notes and --

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: This was a one-day search on the 24th of July, 2002 by four teams of the OTP at several sites in Tuzla, including the 2nd Corps headquarters located in street Ulica Muharema Fizovica and the Husein Kapetan Gradasevic barracks. We were allowed to enter these premises and obtain documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. Now, tell Their Honours how the process of seizing, recording and taking away of the documents occurs.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only talk about the part that I was involved in. To be more specific, I was the team leader of a specific search, and my search team personnel contained investigators and language assistants, and one of the investigators was an evidence custodian. And as a result of the search, as documents were handed over, the evidence custodian recorded the searches in a property -- property seizure register form. It describes -- we assigned a number and described from which shelf and basically a brief description of what the document may contain and the person who handed over the document to the evidence custodian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't want to lead you, but just so that -- I want to be clear. Is it the case that one officer acts the exhibits custodian and keeps this form called a property seizure record and the other officers bring to him documents that they have seized and he then enters details onto that particular form?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true, they way you described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Once that's happened, does he take the documents into his possession?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. The documents are taken into possession and it is stored in a secure place, as I said. On the day later, which was the 25th, we went through the documents again in the presence of the evidence custodian to see -- to make sure that the documents we are taking are really the relevant documents, so to speak. A final -- a final selection before we send the rest of the selection to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And do you know how documents that -- large quantities of documents that are seized in the field in such operations are actually sent back to The Hague or does it differ from -- on each occasion?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: In this case each stack of documents were individually secured with plastic covers and were placed in a large box and sealed in Tuzla. And in this particular mission, we had a member of the evidence unit present with us, and it was easier that way. So he took possession of the seized documents, and he -- it was brought to The Hague in the UN plane, in the custody of the evidence custodian officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court if from your knowledge and based on the experience that you've had here at the Office of the Prosecutor since 1995, the last nine years, whether that procedure is normally adopted in search operations and seizure operations in the field?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the normal procedure. It's a standing -- a standard operating procedure for investigation division which all officers are familiar with the procedures and they comply with it. I should say they should comply with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we've discussed -- you've given evidence of two types of seizure, we'll call them the smaller individual seizure that might be conducted by a single officer who might be interviewing a witness and these larger seizures. I want you to refocus back now on the smaller seizure where a single officer might be seizing one or two or three or a smaller number of documents. Once the officer has taken the document, completed his receipt or written it into the body of the statement, the fact of its receipt, does he keep custody of the document?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. He keeps safe custody of the document until he comes back to the office in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Now, I want you to describe to the Court the process that the officer is required to under -- to complete when he gets back here.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Once the officer gets back to the office, he's -- he or she is supposed to immediately process the documents through our system, which means if the document is in B/C/S, with the help of the language assistant the officer compiles a summary of the document in order to fill in a IIF or a MIF.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They're obviously acronyms. What do they stand for; do you know?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: India India Foxtrot stands for information index form, and MIF, Mike India Foxtrot stands for the mini version of the IIF.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, we might invent new words today, IIFing and MIFing, and so if I use those words, I apologise for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus on the IIF form. Before I do, is there any essential difference between the MIF and the IIF form?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No. It's a mini version of the IIF. Just that -- only the relevant fields are now UFO [phoen]. If Their Honours allow me, I can show you copies of it so you know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a good idea, Mr. Di Fazio. Let's -- if we are going to MIF and IIF, I think we better start with the hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: May I just see one before it's handed up to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't suppose we need these as exhibits. Mr. Jones, we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honour's hands. If you want to mark them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As an exhibit. I mean, we will consider them as evidence in accordance with the guidelines that we gave you yesterday, what we considered to be evidence, items that are just shown to us and which are not really tendered into --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- exhibited, useful to have copies, if we could have copies as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as we are concerned, I don't think we need more exhibits than we have already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's sentiments. We won't -- I'll provide copies to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, the -- I want you to tell the Chamber, the Trial Chamber, of the -- the important information that has to go into a MIF or IIF form. Firstly, the officer fills out the form?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. The officer fills out the form, and of course this is done electronically. The important thing is the document date, the evidence description, in the title --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just a minute. What is an evidence description? Tell the Trial Chamber what --

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Evidence description means the title, if the document has a title. So you describe that. And a summary, a brief summary of the contents of the document and any other comments which the investigator wants to add in the evidence description field which he think it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And does the document -- sorry, let me rephrase that. Does the officer fill in details of the date of seizure, the name of the seizing officer?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And am I correct that the -- I'm not talking about the large seizures now. I'm only talking about the smaller seizures. Is it correct that the officer who fills out the IIF or the MIF form will be the officer who seized it in the field?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true. Or it could be somebody else who he hands it over to. Say, for instance, another member of the team. For instance, he brings a document to work in the team and it becomes too much for one person to do. So another investigator can help out by filling in IIF. But of course he will say he received it from, for instance, from me, the person who gave him the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So if an officer hands on the task of completing a MIF or an IIF to some other officer, is he required to provide the other officer with all the correct information to --

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there an item in the forms that refers to chain of custody?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. Because if it's a chain of custody, the officer has to select the box.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what -- if the officer selects the box, what essentially does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Chain of custody means that once it's chain of custody, the chain has to be maintained all the way, meaning that once it's handed over to the evidence unit and if another officer wants to view the document for -- for his investigation, the document is released from the evidence unit through a chain of custody which is a special register. So it shows that the officer signing it out. So every time the document is signed out it is reflected in this chain of custody. So you know where the -- the movement of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And whenever MIF or IIF forms are completed, is a computer number automatically generated?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. The MIF is -- MIF number is automatically generated, and the ERN number comes later once the documents are handed over to the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want you to tell the Trial Chamber of the process that occurs after the IIF or the MIF form has been filled out. What does the officer then do?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Once the document has been processed through the IIF or the MIF, the actual exhibit or item is taken down to the evidence unit and handed over to the evidence custodian. They have a special register. If Their Honours will allow me to show what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: May I have a quick look at it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought I had it with me. It's probably slipped off. Oh, just wait one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for showing us the form.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: So the -- the officer takes the evidence down to the evidence unit and fills in the evidence register and hands it over to the evidence custodian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: And once that's done, it's in the custody of the evidence unit. A day or two you -- an officer can view the document that he sent down to the evidence unit on the electronic database.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that's the process that occurs in the case of smaller seizures that might be conducted by one or two or three officers. Now, in these larger -- larger seizures that are conducted with a larger number of officers, where many, many documents are involved, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the procedure is there? Again, I'd like to hear the process from the point at which the documents have all been collated and the property seizure record that you referred to has been completed out in the field. What happens from that point onwards?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: As I described earlier, these documents are brought to the evidence unit, and the officer -- well, after they are processed through the evidence unit they acquire ERN numbers. These are unique numbers. And any investigative team can search through the system and pick out documents they wish to use during the investigation. And of course, the documents they take will eventually be added to the investigation. So if they find it relevant, they will -- if a particular document for the evidence of that particular investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've jumped the gun a bit. What I'm actually interested in is the process that occurs from the point at which all the documents have been collated in the field. They've all been collected, put into boxes or whatever, and transported back to The Hague, to the OTP. Now, at this point how does the IIFing take place? Does the individual officer IIFed whatever documents he ceased or is the property seizure record used to create the IIF forms or is it exactly the same as the process you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No, it's not the same. The officer who seized the documents is not necessarily completing the IIF. These large quantity of documents are brought to The Hague. The investigator who is in charge of the investigation or the team members usually undertake the task of IIFing these documents based on the property seizure register I mentioned earlier. On that information, he completes the IIFing or the MIFFing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. So from the property seizure record, anyone can see which officer seized the document concerned and the place and date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And can provide that information to the IIF or the MIF form.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's the way it's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to -- I'm going to deal with something called requests for assistance shortly, but before I do, I just want you to provide some very brief comments about your annex. utterances.text: That's true. This information, I based it on the IIF.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll return to the annex in a little more detail shortly. I now want to ask you about another method of acquiring documentation, and that is the request for assistance. Please tell the Trial Chamber what a request for assistance is.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Request for assistance is when we send out a request to the former Yugoslavia or countries outside the former Yugoslavia for assistance according to our rules and procedure of evidence, which is, I think, 39. These requests are processed by the investigating officer, and it goes through our request unit. When a request is as a result of trial-related matter, it's got to be approved by a senior trial attorney before it goes down to the request unit. And if it's still in its investigative stages, it's got to be approved by the chief of investigation. Once the request is approved by either parties, it goes down to the request unit, and this goes to the respective liaison officers, whether it's the BiH government or the RS, or any other government organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And if the request is accommodated and the government concerned is able to meet the request, say, for example, in the case of a document, will it then send the document here to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It comes through the request unit and from the request unit it's passed on to the specific person who requested for it or to the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just -- I want to get down to the nitty-gritty of the actual details. Once a request has gone out and a reply has been received, the material's been received, and is the material actually sent to the requests unit?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. The requests unit take possession of it because they act in between for the investigator and the liaison office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the material has arrived. It's in the requests unit. What does the requests unit do?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: The request unit, of course when they send it out they log it in, and when it comes in, they log it in and inform the respective investigating officer or the team to take possession of the documents. And one it's in possession of the requested person, that is the investigator on the team, the documents as such is IIFed or MIFFed and processed as part of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Using the procedure that you described before?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So in the case of documents that are obtained through request for assistance, there is no field operation, there is no contact with the person providing the document. The point at which the investigator or the person concerned gets it is from the requests unit. They then take it to the evidence unit and go through the process that you've already described?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to turn to individual items in your spreadsheet, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, Judge Eser would like to put a question which is relevant before we proceed any further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Ms. Manas, you told us that you mostly have been provided with copies. My question is why not with originals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In most cases, Your Honour, we -- originals don't exist. So if there's copies and someone can tell us these are the copies, we take them. If there are originals, because we make copies of the original and ask the parties to keep the original for the sake of the trial. When they come they can use the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: When you had received copies, you told us that you would examine whether the copy is a true copy of the original. What was the process of examining it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm talking about when for instance a witness gives you documentation during an investigation, during the course of an interview, he or she probably has a document, say, for instance, a medical certificate, et cetera. We ask the witness to keep the original and we make a copy. That's what I mean. Examine it and see it's a true copy of the original. But in a large search mission, in most cases we do not come in contact with original documents. Most of them are copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser. Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just following on from the question that Judge Eser asked you, when officers go out into the field either in large searches or in smaller searches involving smaller seizures, is it the case they sometimes get original documents provided to them?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is it the case they sometimes get photocopies or copies of documents provided to them?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if they're given a copy of a document but the person giving them doesn't have the original, I take it there's little that they can do. Now, what they can do in the circumstances is accept the copy of whatever original document it was made from.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. Because later on we can probably trace the original if there is an original.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So many documents that might be referred to as an original document in fact might sometimes be a copy of a document that was given for the first time to someone in the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, just to make it clear, because at the end of the day the bottom line is that we never see the originals here in this courtroom unless it is necessary to have the original brought up from the -- the -- from the place where they are -- they are kept for verification or cross-reference. What you produce here is just photocopies of what you have downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the main that is so, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct. That's mainly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we could be talking also of photocopies of photocopies of photocopies sometimes. So that's to make it clear that this is how it works here, and this is how it has to work, and then if we need to make a confrontation with the original, as happened, for instance, in the Brdjanin case, we needed to do that on several occasions, then we do it. And the Prosecution are asked to bring forward the original that they have, which could be a copy in itself, and then we will do that exercise. But this is just to make things clear, that this is the procedure that we follow here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Thank you. And can I ask you to look now at items -- I'm sorry.

utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I am ready now to proceed to the tendering process.

utterances.text: There's just a couple of matters that I need to point out. utterances.text: You want to tender it now, tender it now. I mean, there is no problem with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine. In that case I seek to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what document you're talking about because obviously we haven't seen it. But if it is so important, tender it now, we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The handwriting experts will touch upon it. And that's why I want it in before they--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So if Your Honours please, can I please tender this document headed order and dated the 11th of December, 1992 numbered 134 of 1992 apparently signed by the accused in this case. Copies are being distributed. It's been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this will be given Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: One is Your Honour P263.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be given Exhibit number P263. So do you have any further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. Once the tendering process is complete, there is just one very brief issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me repeat myself. There is just one very brief issue and I'm grateful to Ms. Sellers for reminding me of it. I'm going to finish my examination-in-chief with this witness, but I want to -- the Trial Chamber to know that we will be applying to recall, if that's the right expression, or call again this witness to undergo the same exercise that we've done this morning at some point I hope at a convenient break and I hope fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we would have expected in the first place anyway, simply because we are pretty sure that this one -- this exercise is not complete. It will not be completed today for sure. So at this point in time, Mr. Jones, I -- you have these options: You can start with your cross-examination straight away and then proceed with a statement indicating the exhibits that the Defence has an objection to for admissibility purposes, or else you can start precisely with this statement and then proceed with the cross-examination. My suggestion is that you start and finish with the cross-examination first so that the witness can then leave and we can deal with the question of objections which need not necessarily be debated in her presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I certainly agree that starting with the cross-examination, then proceeding to our objections would be the most appropriate course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I again thank you, Mr. Jones, and you may proceed. You are now going to be cross-examined by the Defence. Thank you. 23

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Manas, in preparing for today and in preparing your declaration, you referred to the IIF and the MIF forms. Do you additionally have access to any other notes taken by investigators in the course of seizing documents?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, we do. For instance, spreadsheets which are compiled on the field itself while the documents are seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so the IIF form and the MIF form is already a summary of information from various sources?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the information which appears in the column, the final column of Annex I to your declaration, the seizure details, that's -- that's a further summary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's right. It's based on the data that I looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when we look at that column, seizure details, there may be additional information about who some of the people or who some of the places are which you have but which doesn't appear in that column. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: This -- the information that appears in this column is based on the IIF and the MIF and other documents I mentioned, like the spreadsheets, searching through them. I just checked them to see if everything is correct, and based on that I searched the IIF. Of course I go through the original documents first and to whatever documents that support that evidence and then the MIF or the IIF.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I see. It's just to say that obviously there's more information which you might have than appears in this column. So if I ask you about it you might be able to elaborate?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the IIF and the MIF forms. Now, just dealing briefly with individual documents which are handed over, first of all, if the person hands over a document to an investigator, would they normally also explain where they got the document from and how they came to have it?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Naturally, yes. It's embodied in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's common practice that the witness would explain, "I received this document from this source and that's how I come to have it"?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So if that's not in the witness statement, it's -- that information is incomplete?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It wouldn't be in accordance with the proper practice.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. Or it might be recorded elsewhere, for instance in a receipt which is -- for instance, if an investigator is not taking a statement from the witness, maybe an investigative note. So just a receipt given to the person who submitted the document or the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So generally whenever a document, an individual document, is given to an investigator, the information should be available as to where that person got the document from?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. If the information is available to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you have guidelines on that sort of thing as well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are they published guidelines? Were they -- or are they confidential to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Confidential to the OTP. I'm not sure on that, but I think it's an office operating procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to start really by just establishing the parameters of your evidence here today. Your testimony is, essentially, as to the source of documents, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This document from this place or that place?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's right to say, isn't it, that if a document has in any way been manipulated, if a signature has been added or a stamp added, if information has been added to the document later but before it was delivered to the Office of the Prosecutor, that's not something you would know about at all?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No. Unless it's brought to your attention and if the investigator finds the discrepancies, of course we follow further investigation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- explained that, "I've added this signature or I've added this stamp"?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the investigator might not know about that and you wouldn't know about that, if there had been manipulation before it was delivered and the person didn't divulge to you that they had manipulated of the document?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So just to be absolutely clear, if someone sat at home, typed a letter up today but dating it October 1992, they put someone's name, take someone's signature, put it in the collection or hand it to an investigator, that's not something you would know that that had been done. You would just say that was in this collection or this was taken from this person on that occasion. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's also true, isn't it, that you wouldn't know or your testimony doesn't go to the issue of whether a document has actually been received where it appears to have been sent? So in other words, if you have -- sorry. I need to slow down, I think, probably. I'll go very slowly. If you have a document, let's say a letter which states that it's copied to various persons, you wouldn't know whether that document had actually been received in this other location just based on the document yourself, would you? You would just -- you would just include that document in your evidence unit?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: During your searches you come across in document where it was cc'd to the person who received it as a stamp of the office or corresponds in respect of that document, then, yes, you would come to know whether that person actually received that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. It's something you can sometimes discover by other means. But on the face of the documents which you collect, you wouldn't know and you don't necessarily try to establish whether it was received or not?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, on the subject of chain of custody, you've mentioned how the IIF form, I think, has a box on chain of custody. It's right, isn't it, that that's chain of custody, once the document is with the ICTY, with the OTP. It doesn't deal with the chain of custody before the document reached the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: When this comes into the hands of the investigating officer or other personnel from the OTP investigation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that sense, it's a partial chain of custody, isn't it, in the sense that you know the chain of custody from when the OTP gets the document, but from the moment the document was created until the OTP received it, you don't record how many hands it went through?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Of course you try to establish that, and if the information is provided, you make record of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your forms deal only with chain of custody in the OTP, that box which you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: From the time it comes into possession of the OTP investigation staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say it's not a complete black hole. You may have information about where the person claims they got the document from and who they got it from back to the source of the document on some occasions?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But that's not included on this spreadsheet? The spreadsheet deals with when the OTP officer gets the document.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: But on the IIF itself will tell you the originator, the originator, the writer of the document. So if that's available, you fill that field in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: By originator you mean what, the author?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: The author of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Which I imagine is pretty rare?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: In most cases there is an author to a document. You can assess it by the signature or who it is addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In those cases, the author of the document doesn't actually provide you with the document there and then?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It would be very rare?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Not the case. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just before I come to some specific questions, you've spoken of collections, seizing collections versus someone who hands over documents voluntarily to you, individual documents and then requests from the Tribunal. Now, on requests, I understood you to say that if a request is made, then the response is sent to your requests unit in the OTP. Is that always true or presumably on some occasions someone in the field will meet with an official and they'll say, "Here's this document which you requested"?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Well, there's many ways to obtain documents, and one of them is through requests through the other governments as I described during my evidence. And of course during investigation in the field, a person can come up to you and provide you documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Just to clarify, because in your evidence you seem to be saying that RFAs always went straight to your request unit, whereas of course I imagine it must be the case that sometimes an officer in the field receives documents pursuant to an RFA?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Well, that specific incident I was talking about requests for assistance. The other thing you're talking about is when an officer is in the field and somebody approaches him or her and provides documents, or during an interview documents are provided. It's different from an RFA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One further preliminary question, and it's really following up on what the learned Judge Eser asked you. If you have a document which you're provided with, let's say an original, and you then make a copy, is it right to say that you don't actually -- you, the officer or the investigator doesn't certify this copy matches the original I've just copied. That isn't part of the process?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: It is part of the process. It is part of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In any document in the custody of the OTP we'll see a signature saying this -- "I certify this conforms to the original"?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: You can't do that in a large collection. When an investigator is given individual documents in the field, yes, of course we do that. We see the original and certify the copy as a true copy of the original on the reverse side. And in large quantities of documents, you would -- you can do one spreadsheet itemising the documents and a signature to the witness to say it's a true copy of the original. You've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to tender some specific items in your spreadsheet, and I'm working from Annex I which I believe we all have, and that numbering. And I'd like to refer you first to item 16 and 17. And also to your proofing notes, if you have those before you?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, as to the proofing notes, it's in fact on the ERN numbers page. It's really just to clarify this point. In the spreadsheet, it's stated that Dan Perry seized those documents from Banja Luka, various places in Banja Luka. In your note, you say: "Items 16 and 17 show that the documents were seized by RS officials, although I'm not sure." Why are you not sure?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't present. Based on the information provided by the -- on the IIF, I gather that this is what happened. The Prosecutor asked me if I knew these individuals, and that's why I said I do not know them, and I do not know the circumstances surrounding the manner in which Mr. Perry obtained these documents. But based on the information provided, that is what I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's surely true of all the items where you weren't actually present?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were receiving it as a secondary source?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: But from the Tuzla collection, I was present during the search operation. So I'm aware of the procedures that took place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For some reason you have special doubts about items 16 and 17.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: I don't have any special doubts. I -- I cannot -- no, I don't have any doubts about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply --

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: It's simply the information I obtained was from the IIF.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's deal with item 16. And you have Milivoje Ivanisevic providing the document to Dan Perry. Who is he? Who is Mr. Ivanisevic? Is he an official?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: He is an official of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Republika Srpska. If you have your notes and you need to refer to them for more detail, that would be helpful. Do your notes record where he got the document from?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No. Which means I have to go and tell you from a specific IIF, and I don't have that specific IIF with me. Mr. Daniel Perry can answer those questions. I'm not in a position to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understood you had access to notes prepared by the investigators?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Not all notes I have access to. Now, looking a bit further down where you have documents received from Jovicic Trivun. I'm not sure I'm pronouncing that correctly. He's the Republika Srpska liaison officer, isn't he; is that right.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, it's right to say, isn't it, that he's just a conduit? He's a go-between?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Uh-huh, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's not actually the source of the document. He gets the document from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you have information as to where he got the document from in each case? Is it just as a general matter you would record that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...provided to the investigating officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So for the spreadsheet to be complete, you wouldn't say, "We received it from the postman." You would say who you really -- who the source was. That information is available to you?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. Because now I'll have to go and look at the specific RFA 285 and see the response to that, and in that RFA it will tell you where exactly Mr. Jovicic received the documents from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply to clarify what your spreadsheet contains and what other information might be out there. If I could turn to item 38. Now, there, the seize our details that Carolyn Edgerton received that document from Fikret Masic from AID Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the IIF information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've checked that to be correct.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've checked that specific information to be correct?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the IIF information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: AID Sarajevo and the date?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's all correct. Okay. I want to refer you to items 49 to 57. And this concerns the material seized from Colonel Sarenac. And I think your evidence this morning was that that was a seizure. Those documents were seized. It was a collection that was seized.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Does that mean that it wasn't -- it wasn't a voluntary handing over of documents, it was a coercive seizure?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: There were many types of seizures. This was a consensual hand-over done by the authorities themselves. From the notes I've been reading on this, the investigators were present and these documents were brought over to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So in fact, this was more of a selection of documents being handed over by an official than the seizure of a whole collection, like the Sarajevo collection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: It's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we see that that's Colonel Sarenac but then we have a building, a military defence building. Obviously it's not --

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Location. It would be referring to a location.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not just --

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Military defence building, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. But obviously Colonel Sarenac isn't just loitering in the corridors. Presumably he has some position and that building is a government department or something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: For instance, it says Steve Tedder from Colonel Rajko Sarenac means that he received it from this colonel, and the location is a military defence building in Banja Luka, 13th of July, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So my question is: What agency is in that building? What government department does Colonel Sarenac work for? Do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No, I don't. You'd have to ask Mr. Steve Tedder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you don't know why he happens to have all these documents?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I refer you now it items 59 to 94. And these are documents taken from Major Ronko Todorovic. And firstly the same question: Was this a coercive seizure or was this a voluntary handing over of documents?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: It's a voluntary hand-over of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now it appears looking at the description of the documents that they're all to do with imprisonment, with the detention charges in this indictment, interrogations of prisoners mostly. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These documents were taken from the 5th Corps headquarters Sokolac of Republika Srpska. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: That's right. My notes, if you want me to tell you how they got in possession of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Actually, let's take it one step at a time. The 5th Corps, presumably that's a normal army division of the Republika Srpska. Did you have any reason why they have the whole detention file against Naser Oric --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: My learned friend is stretching things a bit there. There's no evidence that they have the whole detention file against Naser Oric. Only the face of the document, it -- the observation can be made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to continue, Mr. Di Fazio. It's objection. Objection sustained. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, do we know what agency, if indeed there is an agency or a division in the 5th Corps, had these documents in its possession? Is that clear from your notes?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: From my notes it says according to -- according to the mission order, the VRS Drina Corps obtained the documents issued by ABiH authorities at some unknown time and transferred them to the VRS 5th Corps headquarters in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the 5th Corps of Republika Srpska received the documents from the Drina Corps, which is a Bosnian Serb army division. They got the documents from the ABiH, the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at some disclosed time, the documents from the enemy during the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You don't know when, all right. But you don't have any further details as to what agency or division within the 5th Corps, whether it's, I don't know, counter-intelligence, propaganda, misinformation, you don't have any details of which specific part of this regular army division had these documents in its custody?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No. I -- I think the investigators who were present during this collection can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, is Dan Perry still in the employ of the Tribunal or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other person that was mentioned earlier, Steve Tedder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He's also not an employee any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the problem that is encountered most of the time, and that's why I suggested in the very beginning to get one person who would make the necessary searches and then try to enlighten us as much as she could, and I think more or less you have -- Madam Manas, you have done a wonderful job.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly. There is never any criticism if Ms. Manas doesn't have -- no information, she relies on the investigator's notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. But it's good to know whether the persons -- because when you tell us you can check it with Dan Perry, well, I mean if we can locate Dan Perry and if need be we can bring him over, yes, but it's also useful to know here and now that he's no longer in the employ of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I could now turn to item 97. Now, there we have a document supplied by the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation. It's also known as NIOD, I believe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the other word that you mentioned. Yes, it was obtained from the Netherlands Institute of War Documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that -- I think I'm right in saying that that's the only document provided by them on your spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That document doesn't appear to be to have been provided in response to a request for assistance. It was voluntarily provided; is that right?

utterances.text: I think we are sitting in the morning but I'm afraid I didn't bring the chart with me. Registrar, could you check that for us, please. But my impression is that we are sitting the entire week in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if Dr. Gow is now scheduled as per our request for Tuesday and Wednesday to give us enough time for the cross-examination. Apologies, Wednesday and Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wednesday and Thursday. Because there's Dr. Koeijer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or whatever his name is. I can inform that we are sitting the entire week in the morning, not in this courtroom, however, in courtroom 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can provide a three-hour time estimate for cross-examining on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thanks a lot. We will reconvene on Monday. Have a nice weekend. And don't tire yourself out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of October, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.07 p.m.,
